## 1. Identification Strategy  

Primary design: Regression Discontinuity Design (RDD).  
•  Institutional fit – the covenant threshold is a pre-specified, contractually fixed number that neither the lender nor the borrower can renegotiate ex-ante. When the realised accounting ratio barely crosses that number, the firm’s legal status with the bank changes discretely, generating a sharp fall in credit supply that is orthogonal to contemporaneous investment opportunities.  
•  Research fit – we need the causal effect of an exogenous reduction in credit supply on financing/investment. An RDD isolates observations just on either side of the threshold, creating quasi-random assignment of the credit shock.  
•  Complementary design – once the local RDD estimate of the immediate shock is obtained, an event-time difference-in-differences (event study) can trace dynamic responses. The core identification, however, relies on the local RDD.

## 2. Treatment and Control  

Treatment variable  
•  Treated = 1 if the firm’s accounting ratio at quarter t is on the “breach” side of its covenant threshold (e.g. Debt/EBITDA – Threshold > 0 for a maximum covenant or Interest-Coverage – Threshold < 0 for a minimum covenant).  
•  Control = 0 if the same firm–quarter observation is on the compliant side but within a chosen bandwidth h of the threshold.

Running variable and cutoff  
•  Running variable r_it = ratio_it – threshold_i (re-sign so that r_it = 0 at cutoff; r_it < 0 = compliant, r_it ≥ 0 = violation).  
•  Cut-off c = 0.

Event date / timing  
•  Quarter (or fiscal month) in which r_it crosses zero is date 0. Outcome variables such as net debt issuance, new loan volume, CAPEX, R&D, acquisition spending, employment, etc. are measured in the same quarter and in subsequent k quarters.  
•  Dynamic DID/event-study specification will use event time τ = –4…+8 relative to first breach.

Counterfactual group  
•  Firms in quarters with −h < r_it < 0 (“just compliant”) serve as the local counterfactual in the RDD.  
•  For the longer-horizon event study we match each breaching firm to the nearest neighbour (Mahalanobis on size, industry, pre-shock leverage) that NEVER breaches during the sample window.

## 3. Key Identifying Assumptions  

A1 – Continuity of potential outcomes at r=0  
  • Investment demand, profitability trends, etc. evolve smoothly in the narrow neighbourhood of the threshold absent treatment.  
  • Plausible because the numeric difference of e.g. Debt/EBITDA of 2.99 vs 3.01 is economically negligible.  

A2 – No precise manipulation of the running variable  
  • Firms may attempt accounting management but cannot deterministically hit 3.00 because EBITDA and debt levels are noisy; covenants are defined on GAAP numbers reviewed by auditors/banks.  

A3 – Treatment status changes discontinuously at cutoff (first-stage relevance)  
  • By contract the lender obtains acceleration rights at breach; historical evidence shows a sharp jump in renegotiation probability.  

A4 – Stable unit treatment value (no spill-overs within the local window)  
  • One firm’s covenant status does not influence the credit supply of a neighbouring firm within the few-basis-point window.  

A5 – Local linearity within chosen bandwidth  
  • The conditional expectation of outcomes is smooth and can be approximated by linear (or low-order polynomial) trends in r.

Given the institutional context (private bilateral contract, preset numbers) these assumptions are reasonable; we will formally test A1–A3.

## 4. Threats to Identification & Mitigations  

1. Strategic manipulation / “window dressing”  
   – McCrary density test for sorting at r=0; compare accruals, working-capital spikes.  
   – Donut RD (drop |r|<0.005) to rule out precise manipulation.  

2. Endogenous covenant setting (tougher lenders pick weak firms)  
   – Covenant level is predetermined long before breach; our RD uses *within-firm* variation around its own threshold, netting out lender selection.  

3. Simultaneous deterioration in fundamentals drives both breach and lower investment (remaining demand confound)  
   – Local continuity test: check profitability growth, Tobin’s q, sales growth trends inside ±h.  
   – Include lagged fundamentals and firm FE in the dynamic DID to soak up residual demand-side trends.  

## 5. R Code Outline  

```r
###############################################################################
# 0. Packages
library(data.table)
library(fixest)      # fast fixed-effect regressions
library(rdrobust)    # robust RD estimation
library(ggplot2)

###############################################################################
# 1. Load and merge data
cov  <- fread("dealscan_covenants.csv")         # loan-level covenants
cs   <- fread("compustat_quarterly.csv")        # firm-quarter accounting
link <- fread("link_table.csv")                 # gvkey-permno link if CRSP used

# Merge Compustat w/ covenant thresholds at the loan level
dat <- merge(cs, cov, by = c("gvkey","fyearq","fqtr"), all.x = TRUE)

###############################################################################
# 2. Variable construction
# Example for a maximum Debt/EBITDA covenant
dat[, runvar := (debt_to_ebitda - covenant_max)]
dat[, treat  := (runvar >= 0)]                        # 1 = breach
# Outcomes
dat[, capex_assets := capx / at]                      # investment intensity
dat[, netdebt_iss  := (dltt - L(dltt,1)) / at]        # Δlong-term debt

# Keep obs with valid running var
dat <- dat[!is.na(runvar) & !is.na(capex_assets)]

###############################################################################
# 3. RD main specification (local linear, Imbens-Kalyanaraman bw)
bw_ik <- IKbandwidth(dat$runvar, dat$capex_assets)$h  # or rdrobust automatic

rd  <- rdrobust(y = dat$capex_assets, x = dat$runvar,
                c = 0, p = 1, kernel = "triangular")

print(summary(rd))

###############################################################################
# 4. Dynamic event-study DID (–4 … +8 quarters)
# Create event time relative to first breach per firm
dat[, first_breach_q := min(quarter[runvar>=0]), by = gvkey]
dat[, tau := quarter - first_breach_q]
dat <- dat[tau >= -4 & tau <= 8]

# Sun & Abraham (2020) style staggered DID
did <- feols(capex_assets ~ i(tau, treat==1, ref = -1) | gvkey + fqtr,
             data = dat)
iplot(did)

###############################################################################
# 5. Robustness: Donut RD excluding |runvar|<0.01
dat2 <- dat[abs(runvar) > 0.01]
rd_donut <- rdrobust(y = dat2$capex_assets, x = dat2$runvar)
summary(rd_donut)
```

## 6. Expected Results  

Economic intuition: loss of credit supply tightens financial constraints →  
•  Net debt issuance should fall sharply (estimate: –5–8 p.p. of assets in the breach quarter).  
•  CAPEX / Assets should drop, perhaps by –1 p.p. (roughly a 15–20 % decline from the mean).  
•  R&D may fall less (more intangible, internally funded).  
Magnitude benchmark: prior literature on loan supply shocks (e.g., Chava/Ojejimi) finds 15–30 % reductions in investment for shocked firms; our local RD window may yield the lower end of that range.

## 7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (RDD)  

C1: Smooth density of running variable at cutoff  … 1  
C2: Covariate balance within chosen bandwidth      … 1  
C3: Correct functional form / bandwidth choice     … 0.5 (sensitivity tested)  
C4: No other discrete policy or contract change at r=0 … 0.5  
C5: First-stage discontinuity strong (breach → higher renegotiation, credit cuts) … 1  

Total ≈ 4/5 – design is solid but relies on careful functional-form checks and ruling out coincident shocks.
